passage: By noon the Holi party in the colony's parking lot had gone loud in a new way. Damini, twenty, noticed it first in the balloons: at eleven they were tossed at friends; now a few boys were aiming them at passing autos and laughing when a driver swerved. Someone had brought a bottle nobody admitted to. Lalremsiami, her hostel roommate, was being pulled toward a tub of purple water by strangers while she shook her head, still smiling politely. A man dragged a chair over to climb the wall. Tomorrow, Damini thought, half these people will scroll past the photos and wince. She took Lalremsiami's wrist, said "Chai break," and walked her out. At the gate she told the society secretary about the autos. He switched off the speaker. The shouting dropped at once.

qa.a: Lalremsiami was probably uncomfortable but stuck being polite, shaking her head yet still smiling while strangers pulled her toward the tub.

"Pooja, come here a sec," Irfan said, pulling her into the stairwell of their building.
"What? It's nearly midnight!"
"Look at the parapet. Three of Kunal's friends are sitting on it with their legs outside."
"They're just having fun."
"An hour ago it was dancing. Now someone threw a glass down into the lane. Did you hear it smash?"
Pooja paused. "Okay... I heard something."
"Everyone's cheering everyone on. Nobody's thinking. Tomorrow they'll be mortified, and one of them could fall."
"So what do we do? It's our party."
"That's why. You turn the music down and bring out the cake. I'll ask them off the wall to light the sparklers."
"Cake at eleven fifty?"
"Early cake beats a broken head."
Pooja laughed, a bit shakily. "Fine. Go."
Five minutes later the parapet was empty, and everyone was crowding around a lopsided chocolate cake.

qa.q: What did someone throw down into the lane?
qa.a: Someone threw a glass down into the lane.

qa.q: What is Irfan worried about?
qa.a: Irfan is worried that people are cheering each other on without thinking, will be mortified tomorrow, and that one of them could fall.

qa.q: What plan turned the rooftop party around, and why did it work?
qa.a: Pooja turned down the music and brought out the cake while Irfan asked people off the wall to light sparklers; it gave the crowd a new focus without a fight 🙂

qa.q: Why did Pooja first say they were just having fun?
qa.a: From inside the party, Pooja had not noticed the slide from dancing to recklessness until Irfan pointed at the parapet and the smashed glass.

grounding: Illustrates flatmates hosting a New Year party who spot the mood turning reckless and redirect it before anyone gets hurt.

passage: I'm Jagdish, and last month I learned something about crowds at our college fee protest. It started well: slogans, songs, Preeti with her hand-painted banner. By the time we reached the admin block, though, the chants had changed. Somebody started kicking the gate. A second-year boy picked up a brick 'just to hold'. I felt the pull too; my own voice was getting louder and meaner, and I didn't recognise the words coming out. That scared me more than the brick. I told Preeti, "This isn't us anymore." She looked around and nodded. We went to the front and started the slow song from the morning again. About thirty people joined. The brick went back on the ground. Looking back, noticing early was what mattered; ten minutes later, I don't think anyone would have listened.

qa.q: What did a second-year boy pick up?
qa.a: A second-year boy picked up a brick 'just to hold'.

qa.q: What scared Jagdish more than the brick, and why?
qa.a: Jagdish's own voice getting louder and meaner, with words Jagdish didn't recognise, was scarier because it showed the crowd was pulling at Jagdish too.

qa.q: What choice did Jagdish and Preeti make at the admin block?
qa.a: They went to the front and started the slow song from the morning again; about thirty people joined and the brick went back on the ground.

qa.q: What would change if they had waited ten more minutes?
qa.a: Jagdish thinks nobody would have listened by then, so the protest might have slid into damage people would regret.

grounding: Shows a student at a protest seeing the mood turn reckless, feeling the pull, and calming others while it was still possible.

passage:
Coach's note, 3 February. Written by Kamal, women's hockey coach.

We won the inter-college final today, and I'm writing this down because of what Arohi, our twenty-year-old centre half, did afterwards. The team piled into the stadium car park to celebrate. Music, dancing, all good. Around seven someone brought out a big bag of firecrackers, and within ten minutes girls were throwing lit crackers at each other's feet, and two were climbing the team bus to set off rockets from the roof. People were laughing in a way that didn't sound like them. Arohi saw it early. She took the cracker bag, handed it to me, and called the team into a circle for a photo with the trophy, away from the bus. They came. Nobody got hurt.

My next step: I've thanked Arohi in front of the team and asked her to help plan how we celebrate next time.

qa.q: What were two players climbing to set off rockets?
qa.a: They were climbing the team bus to set off rockets from the roof.

qa.q: What did Arohi seem to notice about her teammates' mood?
qa.a: She noticed the celebration had turned reckless, with people laughing in a way that did not sound like them, and seemed to sense they would regret it.

qa.q: Why was calling the team for a trophy photo a smart move?
qa.a: It gave everyone a happy reason to step away from the bus and the crackers without scolding anyone, so the mood calmed quickly.

qa.q: How might the players who were throwing crackers see it the next day?
qa.a: They may feel embarrassed and relieved, realising how close someone came to getting hurt at a happy moment.

grounding: A young player notices a victory celebration sliding from festive to reckless and calmly moves her team away before anyone gets hurt.

passage:
Sunday, very late.

India won the final tonight and the whole city came out. Minakshi and I went down to the big crossing near our girls' PG with our faces painted. For the first hour it was lovely: strangers hugging, drums, people handing out sweets.

Then it changed. Some boys started rocking a stopped bus with people still inside. Others climbed a traffic signal. A group was shaking a scooter while the rider begged them to stop, and people were filming instead of helping. The cheering got a hard edge. I looked at Minakshi and she was cheering at the bus too, without seeming to notice.

I thought: tomorrow half these people will see those videos and feel sick.

I said, "Let's go, now," and pulled her into a side lane. From the gate I called the police helpline about the bus. Minakshi kept saying, "It was just fun." At home she went quiet.

- Sharmila

qa.q: What were some boys doing to the stopped bus?
qa.a: They were rocking it with people still inside.

qa.q: What was Sharmila thinking when she saw the crowd change?
qa.a: She was thinking that many of these people would see the videos tomorrow and feel sick, so she knew the fun had turned into something they would regret.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do once she saw the mood shift, and why did timing matter?
qa.a: She left at once with Minakshi and called the police helpline about the bus; acting early meant they were out before the crowd got worse.

qa.q: How might Minakshi see the evening once she goes quiet at home?
qa.a: Minakshi may be starting to realise she was swept along, cheering at something she would never support on her own.

grounding: A young woman at a victory celebration sees the mood turn reckless, understands people will regret it, and leaves with her friend and alerts help.
